analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal child care entitlement for children under six and caps what families pay on a sliding scale.
analysis.headline: Introduced July 15, 2025 with 107 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, where no further action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make child care for children under six an entitlement: any eligible child in a participating state would be guaranteed a slot, with families above roughly the state median income paying no more than 7% of their income and lower-income families paying nothing. The federal government would pay 90% of the cost of direct services and require that provider payments cover the true cost of care, including a living wage for child care staff equal to what elementary educators with similar credentials earn. It also funds startup, quality, and facilities grants to expand the supply of providers, plus $20 billion for local child care grants and Head Start expansion in states that choose not to participate.
analysis.who_benefits: Working families with children under 6, especially low- and middle-income households now paying market-rate child care costs, and the early childhood workforce, whose wages would be required to reach educator-comparable levels.

how_it_helps.text: Beginning October 1, 2026, every eligible child under 6 in a state with an approved plan would be entitled to child care assistance, not just those who win a scarce subsidy slot.
Families at or below 85% of their state's median income would pay no copayment, and no family would pay more than 7% of income toward child care.

States would have to set provider payment rates high enough to cover the full cost of care, including fixed costs and a living wage for staff at least equal to what elementary educators with similar credentials and experience earn.

The bill funds startup and supply expansion grants, quality grants, and facilities grants for providers, with priority for underserved communities, and appropriates $20 billion for grants to localities and Head Start expansion in states that do not take part.

Children with disabilities, infants and toddlers with disabilities, children experiencing homelessness, children in foster or kinship care, and other underserved populations would be prioritized for access and inclusive care.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through open-ended appropriations ('such sums as may be necessary' each year through fiscal 2031) with no offsetting revenue in the bill; states would also cover 10% of direct service costs, half of administration, and must maintain their existing child care spending.

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates unlimited sums 'as may be necessary' through fiscal 2031 with no revenue offsets, so the full cost lands on federal deficits or future tax decisions.

Providers, including home-based family child care businesses, must meet new licensing, quality-tier, and educator-equivalent wage requirements within about 3.5 years or lose eligibility, a compliance burden that could push some small providers out of the market.

States would have to restructure existing child care funding: no more than 15% of current block grant funds could serve children under 6 once the new program starts, and maintenance-of-effort rules limit states' flexibility.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to families is direct and large: child care is one of the biggest household expenses, and the sliding-fee scale plus guaranteed eligibility addresses both price and access. The honest cost is fiscal: an open-ended entitlement with no revenue in the bill, plus wage mandates that raise the cost of care for providers and taxpayers even as they fix a chronically underpaid workforce. Small home-based providers face the hardest transition. The tradeoff is a genuine policy choice about the size of the federal commitment, not a hidden giveaway.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the House Education and Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced, and it has sat there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert C. 'Bobby' Scott (D-VA) introduced the Child Care for Working Families Act in the House on July 15, 2025.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce the same day.
107 House members cosponsored the bill, all of them Democrats; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored it.
Since the referral, the committee has taken no further action on the bill, and the current Congress runs through January 3, 2027.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead:
So far, no one has gained or lost: the bill has not advanced, so families continue paying market child care prices and providers continue operating without new federal support. The status quo persists because the committee has not acted on it in the roughly six months since introduction. The committee majority's inaction leaves things unchanged for now; the bill remains alive through the end of the current Congress in January 2027 but has shown no movement toward a vote, which is the typical path for a one-party bill referred to committee without bipartisan support in a chamber controlled by the other party.

## Sides

For: Rep. Robert C. 'Bobby' Scott (D-VA), House sponsor, direct, record, [S1, S4] introduced the bill. 107 House Democrats, cosponsors, direct, record, [S3] all cosponsored.

Against: House Education and Workforce Committee majority (Republican-controlled), direct, record, [S4] referred the bill on July 15, 2025 and has taken no action since.

Party line: party_line — All 107 cosponsors are Democrats and no Republican has signed on, and the bill sits with the Republican-majority committee.

## Industries

1. Child care providers (centers and family child care businesses) — entrenched, aligned: The bill would make licensed providers the permanent delivery channel for a new federal child care entitlement, routing all assistance and a guaranteed revenue stream through them while also imposing licensing, quality-tier, and wage requirements. Their financial interest and families' interest in affordable care run together here.

2. Early childhood educators and child care staff — gains, aligned: The bill requires payment rates sufficient to fund a living wage for all staff, set at parity with elementary educators with similar credentials, directly targeting the sector's chronically low pay and turnover.

3. Head Start agencies — gains, aligned: The bill appropriates $20 billion for local grants and authorizes awards to Head Start agencies to expand programs in states that do not participate in the new entitlement.

4. Family (home-based) child care providers — mixed, aligned: They would gain access to startup, quality, and facilities grants and technical assistance, but face a 3.5-year deadline to meet new licensing and wage standards or lose eligibility, which could squeeze the smallest operations.

## Scores

public_stakes: 9 — affordable child care for children under 6 is one of the largest household expenses for working families, and guaranteed access plus a 7%-of-income cap would be a major change.

concentrated_stakes: 6 — the child care sector would gain a multi-billion-dollar permanent federal revenue stream and mandatory wage parity, though the industry is diffuse small businesses and nonprofits rather than a few large firms.

outcome_against_public: 5 — what has happened so far is six months of committee inaction on a bill that would substantially lower family costs; nothing has been defeated outright, but no progress has been made either.

support_mismatch: 5 — 107 cosponsors is substantial apparent support, but it is entirely one-sided (all Democrats), and the bill has not received even a hearing, let alone a vote.

corruption_relevance: 1 — the bill concerns child care funding and affordability, not ethics, lobbying, or self-dealing by officeholders.

confidence: 0.9 — the bill text, cosponsor list, and action history are all from official congressional sources and directly support the description; only the trajectory involves judgment about a low-action bill.

categories: social_safety_net, wages_and_labor

trajectory: With a Republican House majority, zero Republican cosponsors, and no committee action since the July 2025 referral, the bill is unlikely to get a markup or floor vote in this Congress; similar versions of the Child Care for Working Families Act introduced in recent Congresses also died without action.
